## The architectural shift: from warehouses to lakehouses

To understand where we are today, we have to look at how data storage
evolved. Historically, organizations moved through three distinct eras.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A["Enterprise Data Warehouse<br>1990s–2010s"] --> B["Data Lake<br>2010s–2020s"]
    B --> C["Data Lakehouse<br>Present"]
```

**The Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) era (1990s–2010s).** Companies stored
clean, highly structured data in rigid SQL databases. It was excellent for
generating basic business reports, but it was incredibly expensive to scale
and completely incapable of handling unstructured data like audio, video, or
massive JSON logs.

**The Data Lake era (2010s–2020s).** With the birth of Hadoop and cloud object
storage (like Amazon S3), companies started dumping everything — raw,
structured, and unstructured data — into a cheap storage pool. While scalable,
these lakes lacked control. With no data validation or transactional safety,
they quickly degraded into disorganized **"data swamps."**

**The Modern Data Lakehouse era (present).** This is the current gold
standard. A Lakehouse implements a specialized storage layer — open-source
columnar frameworks like **Delta Lake** or **Apache Iceberg** — directly on
top of cheap cloud storage. It gives you the best of both worlds: the
ultra-low cost and flexibility of a Data Lake, combined with the strict
reliability, schema enforcement, and ACID transactions of a traditional Data
Warehouse.

## Core architectural principle: decoupling compute from storage

In legacy systems, Compute (the processor that does the heavy lifting,
calculating, and transforming) and Storage (the hard drives where the raw
data sits) were physically bundled inside the same server box. If you ran out
of processing power, you had to buy more storage. If you ran out of storage,
you had to buy more processors. It was expensive and wasteful.

A modern data architecture completely unties these two components so they can
live in separate places and scale independently:

- **The storage layer.** All your data — petabytes of text, numbers, images,
  video — is dumped into an ultra-cheap, infinitely expandable cloud storage
  "lake" (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage). It just sits there safely,
  requiring almost zero electricity or processing power just to hold the
  data, so it costs pennies.
- **The compute layer.** Processing engines (Apache Spark, Databricks) live
  entirely separately. When a data scientist or an AI model needs to run a
  massive computation, a cluster of virtual computers instantly wakes up,
  hooks into the storage layer, pulls the exact data it needs, processes it in
  parallel, and delivers the answer.

### Why this matters

- **Massive cost savings.** If your company collects data 24/7 but only runs
  heavy AI models or reports once a week, you don't need thousands of
  expensive processors sitting idle all week. You pay a tiny fee to store the
  data, spin up 100 virtual computers for the 2 hours it takes to run your AI
  models, and then shut them down completely — you pay for compute by the
  second it actually runs.
- **Infinite scalability.** If a sudden business need requires analyzing 10
  years of data by tomorrow morning, you don't buy new hardware — you command
  500 cloud computers to team up, attack the storage lake simultaneously,
  finish in minutes, and disappear.
- **No single point of failure.** Because your data isn't trapped inside the
  specific computer doing the work, a crashed compute server doesn't lose or
  corrupt anything. The data is safe in the storage layer, and another
  compute server can instantly step in.

In short: decoupling compute from storage turns your data infrastructure from
a rigid, expensive box into a flexible system where storage is your permanent
memory bank, and compute is a powerful muscle you only flex — and pay for —
exactly when you need it.

## Data ingestion: the revolution of ELT over ETL

Both ETL and ELT move raw data from its sources (a mobile app, a website, a
database) into a central storage system where data scientists and AI models
can use it. The letters stand for:

- **Extract** — gathering the raw data from its source
- **Load** — sending the data to its destination
- **Transform** — cleaning, formatting, and preparing the data

The revolution comes down to flipping the order of the last two steps.

**The traditional way — ETL (Extract → Transform → Load).** Extract grabs raw
data directly from production databases. Because legacy database storage was
expensive, engineers then used a separate middle-tier server to clean,
aggregate, and shrink the data *before* storing it, then pushed the
pre-formatted, clean data into a rigid Data Warehouse.

**The modern way — ELT (Extract → Load → Transform).** Pull raw, messy data
from all company sources and instantly dump it into a cloud data pool (Amazon
S3, Google Cloud Storage, Snowflake) in its native, raw state — JSON, Parquet,
CSV, no changes made. When analysts or AI models need the data, distributed
compute engines (Apache Spark, dbt) transform and clean it inside the storage
destination itself, on demand.

| Feature | Legacy ETL | Modern ELT |
|---|---|---|
| Speed of ingestion | Slow — data waits to be transformed before it can be saved | Ultra-fast — raw data is dumped into storage within seconds |
| Data preservation | Lossy — raw details are thrown away during transformation | Preserved — 100% of raw historical data is saved forever |
| Flexibility | Low — changing the pipeline means redesigning the whole system | High — a new format is just a new query against the raw data |
| Failure recovery | Hard — a mid-pipeline failure can lose or strand data | Easy — raw data stays safe in storage; fix the script and rerun |

In short, the revolution of ELT over ETL is a shift from "clean it before you
keep it" to "keep it all, and clean it whenever you need it." By leveraging
cheap cloud storage and massive compute, ELT ensures modern AI systems always
have access to a rich, uninterrupted history of raw information.

## ACID transactions

**ACID** — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — is a fundamental
set of four safety properties that guarantee database operations remain
reliable and error-free, even during sudden crashes, power failures, or
simultaneous user errors. A **transaction** is a sequence of multiple
database actions treated as a single logical unit of work.

Without ACID guardrails, if a multi-step update hits a network glitch halfway
through, the system can save a partial, broken file that permanently
corrupts your records. ACID compliance protects the whole ecosystem from data
corruption by treating data mutations with strict, absolute validation rules:

- **Atomicity** — an all-or-nothing rule. If a pipeline updating 100 rows
  fails on row 99, the entire operation is rolled back as if it never
  happened. No partial writes.
- **Consistency** — any data written strictly obeys predefined structural
  blueprints, schema enforcement, and database constraints before it's
  committed to storage.
- **Isolation** — when multiple pipelines or users concurrently modify the
  same data lake, their transactions run independently without overlapping or
  cross-contaminating each other's live files.
- **Durability** — once a transaction is successfully written, its changes
  are permanently recorded in non-volatile storage and transaction logs. The
  clean data is never lost, even after a catastrophic power failure.

## Delta Lake

**Delta Lake** is an open-source storage management layer installed directly
on top of a standard cloud data lake (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage) to
turn it into a highly organized, reliable Data Lakehouse. Historically, data
lakes let companies store massive volumes of raw files cheaply, but they
lacked management controls and degraded into "data swamps" where simultaneous
file updates could corrupt information. Delta Lake fixes this by wrapping raw
files in a protective engine that brings database-style reliability, strict
data quality controls, and fast SQL query performance to your existing cloud
storage — all while keeping the lake's ultra-low operational cost.

The engine achieves this through three core technical guardrails:

- **ACID compliance** — an all-or-nothing gatekeeper. If a computer crashes
  mid-pipeline, a half-written file is safely rolled back instead of
  permanently corrupting the database.
- **The Delta Log** — a hidden central ledger recording a perfect historical
  diary of every data mutation. This powers **Time Travel**, letting
  engineers instantly query or restore the dataset exactly as it looked at
  any point in the past.
- **Schema enforcement** — validates the structure of all incoming streams at
  the door, blocking malformed data before it can crash downstream ML models
  or dashboards.

You don't choose *between* Delta Lake and ACID transactions — you use Delta
Lake *because* it provides ACID transactions on top of cheap cloud object
storage. It turns a chaotic, unsafe data lake into a reliable,
enterprise-ready lakehouse.

| | Delta Lake | ACID transactions |
|---|---|---|
| What is it? | An open-source storage layer built on top of file systems | A theoretical standard of data integrity and reliability |
| Implementation | You install it, write code with it, and store files (Delta tables) | A checklist of guarantees implemented by the storage engine |
| Mechanism | Parquet files + an immutable `_delta_log` file tracker | Write-ahead logs, locking mechanisms, isolation levels |
| Scope | Specific to the Big Data / Cloud Lakehouse ecosystem | Applies globally to all databases, financial systems, storage engines |

### The Delta transaction log: how ACID actually works

`_delta_log/` is a hidden directory of JSON commit files at the root of every
Delta table. Each commit is one atomic operation — add new Parquet files,
remove old ones, never a partial write. The read protocol replays every
commit from version 0 to reconstruct the current table state.

Writers use **optimistic concurrency control**: they check for conflicting
commits before finalizing a write. If two writers race on the same partition,
one wins and one retries — no corruption, no data loss. This is how Delta
guarantees ACID without a traditional database engine underneath it.

After every 10 commits, Delta writes a `checkpoint.parquet` so readers don't
have to replay thousands of JSON files on startup — this is Delta Log
compaction.

### `MERGE` / `UPSERT` — why overwrite is not enough

A raw overwrite rewrites the entire table for one changed row: O(n) cost, no
history, unsafe under concurrency. `MERGE` is the operation that makes atomic
upserts possible:

```sql
MERGE INTO target USING source ON condition
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
```

Delta executes `MERGE` atomically: it scans only the affected files, writes
new Parquet, and logs the operation. The typical use case is **CDC (Change
Data Capture)** — applying inserts, updates, and deletes from a source system
in one pass. **Predicate pushdown** lets Delta skip files whose min/max stats
prove no matching rows exist, which is a massive speedup. Combine `MERGE`
with timestamp columns for **SCD Type 2** — full history without duplicates
or missing records.

### `OPTIMIZE` and `Z-ORDER BY` — data skipping

Streaming writes create thousands of tiny Parquet files — the **small files
problem** — and each file read is a separate I/O operation that kills query
scan time.

- `OPTIMIZE table` compacts small files into larger ones (default target
  ~1 GB) within each partition.
- `Z-ORDER BY (col1, col2)` co-locates related values in the same files using
  space-filling curves. Every file's `_delta_log` entry records min/max stats
  per column, so a reader skips irrelevant files entirely — e.g. `WHERE
  country = 'SA'` reads under 5% of files if the table is Z-ordered by
  `country`.

Schedule `OPTIMIZE` weekly or after bulk loads — running it too frequently
has diminishing returns.

### `VACUUM` and Time Travel — storage management

Old Parquet files stay on disk until explicitly cleaned; Delta just stops
referencing them. That's what makes Time Travel possible:

```sql
SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF 5
SELECT * FROM table TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-01-01'
```

`VACUUM table RETAIN 168 HOURS` deletes files older than the retention window
(default 7 days). **`VACUUM` is irreversible** — deleted files cannot be
restored from Delta. Never vacuum below 7 days if streaming readers are still
active; they may reference older offsets. Longer retention means richer time
travel history, at the cost of a higher object storage bill.

### Schema evolution — handling upstream changes

By default, Delta rejects writes with schema mismatches — this protects
downstream queries from silent corruption. To opt in to schema evolution:

- `spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled", "true")`
- `mergeSchema=True` on write — adds new columns from the source, never drops
  existing ones.
- `overwriteSchema=True` — a full schema replacement, for intentional
  breaking changes only.

Schema enforcement happens at **write time, not read time** — errors surface
at the producer, not the consumer. Best practice: version schema changes, and
notify consumers before adding `NOT NULL` columns or renaming fields.

## Lab: build a local mini-lakehouse using Delta Lake

The [Day 1 lab notebook](Day1_Lab.ipynb) simulates a production environment
using Apache Spark (via PySpark) and Delta Lake, demonstrating every concept
above end to end: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, `MERGE`,
`OPTIMIZE`/`Z-ORDER`, `VACUUM`, Time Travel, and schema evolution — on a real,
executed run.

**Requirements.** Delta Lake requires PySpark; the lab also installs
`delta-spark`, which hooks the Delta engine into the Spark session:

```
pyspark==3.5.0
delta-spark==3.5.0
```

**The implementation.** The notebook initializes a local Spark session
configured with Delta Lake, creates a mock e-commerce transaction dataset,
then walks through the mechanics covered above on that real data: it enforces
schema on write, runs updates securely, and rolls the table back using Time
Travel.

What to look for in the output:

- The Delta Lake engine automatically catches a malicious schema deviation and
  causes a controlled crash, demonstrating how it prevents your production
  Data Lake from degrading into a disorganized "data swamp."
- The history ledger maps out exact version numbers — version 0 for the
  initial write, version 1 for the follow-up append — along with timestamps
  and operations (`WRITE` / `APPEND`), showing how easy it is to perform
  point-in-time rollbacks for auditing or ML reproducibility.

::: {.callout-note}
Running the Delta Lake part of this notebook locally on Windows requires a
`winutils.exe` / `HADOOP_HOME` setup for PySpark — a standard PySpark-on-Windows
limitation, not a bug in the notebook. It runs cleanly on Colab (Linux) or
macOS/Linux with no extra setup.
:::
